title: Ecology Basics
summary: This lesson introduces the concept of ecosystems and how living things interact within them. It explains food webs, energy flow, and the major types of biomes on Earth.

sections.heading: What Is an Ecosystem?
sections.body:
An ecosystem is a community of organisms living together with the non‑living things around them, such as water, soil, and climate. The biotic (living) and abiotic (non‑living) parts constantly influence each other.

For example, a pond ecosystem includes fish, algae, insects, water, sunlight, and the temperature of the water. Changes in any one part—like a drop in temperature—affect the whole system.

sections.heading: Food Webs and Energy Flow
sections.body:
Energy enters an ecosystem as sunlight, which producers (plants and algae) capture through photosynthesis. Herbivores eat the producers, carnivores eat the herbivores, and decomposers break down dead material.

A food web shows many feeding relationships at once, illustrating how energy moves through different pathways. Only about 10% of the energy passes from one trophic level to the next; the rest is lost as heat or used for life processes.

sections.heading: Major Biomes
sections.body:
Biomes are large regions with similar climate, plants, and animals. Common biomes include forests, deserts, grasslands, tundra, and aquatic biomes like oceans and freshwater lakes.

Each biome has a characteristic set of adaptations. For instance, cacti store water in deserts, while polar bears have thick fur and fat to survive in the tundra.

key_terms.meaning: A community of living organisms interacting with their physical environment.
An organism, usually a plant or algae, that makes its own food using sunlight.
A step in a food chain, such as producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, etc.
A large area with a distinct climate and characteristic plants and animals.
Organisms like fungi and bacteria that break down dead material and recycle nutrients.
A diagram that shows the decreasing amount of energy available at each successive trophic level.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes an ecosystem?
options: A single species living in isolation
A group of animals that hunt together
A community of organisms interacting with non‑living factors
A laboratory experiment on plant growth
quiz.why: An ecosystem includes both living organisms and their physical environment.

quiz.q: What percentage of energy typically passes from one trophic level to the next?
quiz.why: Only about 10% of energy is transferred; the rest is lost as heat or used for metabolism.

quiz.q: Which biome is characterized by very low temperatures and permafrost?
quiz.why: The tundra has cold temperatures and permanently frozen ground (permafrost).
Decomposers recycle nutrients by breaking down dead material.

flashcards.back: A community of organisms plus the non‑living environment they interact with.
An organism that makes its own food from sunlight (e.g., plants).
A step in a food chain, such as producer, primary consumer, etc.
A large area with a specific climate and typical plant and animal life.
Shows how energy decreases at each higher trophic level, usually about 10% transfer.
